causal_agent: Passalora fulva (syn. Fulvia fulva, Cladosporium fulvum)
distribution: Worldwide; especially problematic in greenhouses and high tunnels with high humidity

leaves: Yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces
Fuzzy olive-green to gray mold growth on lower leaf surfaces
Leaves may curl and become distorted
stems: Occasionally stems can be infected, but disease is mostly foliar

disease_cycle: Spores form on lower leaf surfaces within 10–12 days of infection
High relative humidity (≥85%) favors spore production and infection
Multiple generations can occur within a single growing season
Spread occurs via wind, rain/overhead irrigation, tools, workers, and possibly insects
Pathogen can persist in crop residue and on contaminated greenhouse surfaces
environmental_conditions: Optimal temperature: 21–24 °C (70–75 °F), but disease can develop between 10–32 °C (50–90 °F)
High relative humidity (>85%) is critical for severe epidemics
Poor air circulation and leaf wetness favor infection

cultural: Use drip irrigation and avoid wetting foliage
Space plants to improve air circulation
Stake, string, or prune plants to reduce humidity around leaves
Circulate air in greenhouses/high tunnels with vents, fans, or by rolling up sides
Maintain night temperatures higher than outside to reduce dew formation
Remove and destroy crop residue at the end of the season; sanitize greenhouse surfaces and equipment
resistant_varieties: Use resistant cultivars cautiously, as resistance is often race-specific
Test resistant varieties on a small scale before large-scale planting
Reference: Cornell Disease Resistant Vegetable Varieties list
chemical: Apply fungicides preventively when conditions favor disease
Rotate chemical families to prevent resistance development
For organic production, copper-based products (e.g., Champ) can provide partial control
Follow all pesticide labels and legal restrictions for greenhouse/high tunnel use

notes: Early scouting during high humidity periods is critical for timely management
New races of P. fulva may emerge, so monitoring resistant cultivar efficacy is important
Effective management combines cultural, genetic, and chemical strategies
references: Midwest Vegetable Production Guide for Commercial Growers, 2023
Minnesota Extension, Tomato Leaf Mold Management
Jones, J.B., et al. 2014. Compendium of Tomato Diseases and Pests, 2nd Edition. APS Press.
